text: Morris Kight (November 19, 1919 – January 19, 2003) was an American gay rights pioneer and peace activist, recognized as one of the original founders of the gay and lesbian civil rights movement in the United States. Born and raised in Comanche County, Texas, he graduated from Texas Christian University in 1941 with a degree in personnel administration and public administration. From 1941 to 1958, he lived in northern New Mexico, where he and other gay individuals supported Adlai Stevenson's 1952 presidential campaign, contributing to a rumor that Stevenson was gay. During this time, he married and had two daughters, Carol Kight-Fyfe and Angela Chandler, though he shared this information only with his closest friends, believing it would reduce his credibility as a gay rights advocate. In Albuquerque, from 1950 to 1955, he participated in the "Summerhouse Theater" and "Old Town Players," where he first encountered homophile organizations like the Mattachine Society through actors from California, which he found elitist. Kight was active in various political, civil rights, and labor rights groups, including organizing the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers International Union in the 1940s. After moving to Los Angeles in 1958, he co-founded numerous gay and lesbian organizations, including the militant Committee for Homosexual Freedom (CHF) with Leo Laurence, Gale Whittington, Mother Boats, and others, which later became the Gay Liberation Front (GLF) in October 1969—the third GLF in the U.S. (after New York City and Berkeley)—using the name to show solidarity with the Vietnamese National Liberation Front. By the following year, there were over 350 GLF organizations nationwide. He co-founded the Christopher Street West gay pride parade in 1970, Aid For AIDS in 1983, the Gay Community Center in 1971 (now the Los Angeles Gay and Lesbian Center), the Stonewall Democratic Club in 1975, and hosted the first Asian/Pacific Gays and Friends meetings in his home. Kight led the 1987 Second National March on Washington for Lesbian and Gay Rights and helped organize the 1988 March on Sacramento, where Leonard Matlovich delivered his final public speech. He served on the Los Angeles County Human Relations Commission for two decades. In 2003, the City of Los Angeles dedicated the corner of Hollywood Boulevard and McCadden Place as "Morris Kight Square," chosen as the starting point for Christopher Street West, the world’s first street-closing gay pride parade. In 1998, just before his 79th birthday, West Hollywood’s City Council awarded him a Lifetime Achievement Award. In September 2001, he made a video documentary with West Hollywood Public Access host James Fuhrman titled "Early Gay and Lesbian History in Los Angeles," which included his recollections of the Barney's Beanery protest and other actions. He had a longtime companion named Roy Zucheran. Three days before his death, he donated his memorabilia and archives to the National Gay and Lesbian Archives in Los Angeles, with some archives held by UCLA. He died peacefully at the Carl Bean Hospice in Los Angeles on January 19, 2003. Season 3, episode 8 of the podcast “Making Gay History” features Morris Kight. The Christopher Street West/Los Angeles Gay Pride Morris Kight Lifetime Achievement Award was first given in 2003. A Chinese magnolia tree and a bronze plaque dedicated to him are located at the Matthew Shepard Triangle in West Hollywood, where he regularly visited to tidy, water, and plant flowers, encouraging others to do the same.
